items.title: Thoughtworks Radar Volume 35 turns 'harness engineering' into its own theme — 117 blips, four themes, agent sandboxing moved from Trial to Adopt, and a caution against defaulting to a frontier model for every task
items.summary: On November 4, 2026, Thoughtworks published Volume 35 of its twice-yearly Technology Radar — the industry report that groups software-engineering techniques, tools, platforms, and languages into Adopt, Trial, Assess, and Hold rings. The edition contains 117 blips organized under four named themes: harness engineering at scale; putting more agents to work; beyond frontier models; and the economics of running AI at scale (some Thoughtworks materials call the fourth theme 'the AI factory,' so the naming differs by source). The headline theme is harness engineering — the controls, feedback loops, and infrastructure that wrap around AI coding agents to constrain their behavior and surface errors before they land in production. Thoughtworks' editors say they debated whether to include it as an individual blip but chose to elevate it to a theme because it connects many of the techniques and technologies they're tracking in this edition. Volume 35's other themes push on AI infrastructure economics (Thoughtworks argues token economics are ultimately infrastructure economics — routing, batching, storage, networking, and scheduling all affect production AI costs) and governance for AI-assisted development as adoption scales up. CTO Rachel Laycock is quoted framing the overall question: whether anyone can trust, review, and afford what AI systems produce. New overnight (via post-digest searches and secondary follow-up coverage): the Radar's ring movements in this edition include agent sandboxing moving from Trial to Adopt — a signal that running AI coding agents inside restricted environments is now Thoughtworks' default recommendation rather than an experimental practice — with threat modeling tracking alongside it. The Radar's own Volume 35 page cautions against defaulting to a frontier model for every task, which aligns with the 'beyond frontier models' theme and implies a shift toward task-appropriate model selection rather than one-size-fits-all top-tier calls. A New Stack commentary and companion podcast interview with Thoughtworks' Vanitha Kumar describe harness engineering as equipping agents with automated tests, feedback loops, and guardrails; Kumar's framing is that security will be a dominant topic, and a separate Thoughtworks blog argues the harness is shifting from an implementation detail into a product that needs active ownership — few organizations have a 'harness strategy' yet, while many already have model and platform strategies. The Radar's own notes call out GitHub Spec-Kit and OpenSpec as examples of feedforward controls (spec-driven development frameworks that guide agents through planning, design, and implementation before code is generated) and mutation testing as a feedback control (seeding small intentional bugs into code to check whether the test suite catches them). The edition follows Volume 34 (April 2026), which examined the friction and risks of using AI at scale; Volume 35 is framed as turning from characterization of the problem to managing it. Vendor press-release coverage via ITBrief, SecurityBrief, and ITWire describes the broader argument as a call to return to engineering fundamentals to counter what Thoughtworks calls 'cognitive debt' — the backlog of unexamined, hard-to-reason-about code that accumulates when AI generation outpaces review.
items.why_it_matters: For a hobbyist Python coder using Claude Code, Cursor, or any agent-backed editor, the 'harness' is already the thing that's holding your productivity together even if you haven't named it: your prompt scaffolding, your test suite, the git hooks that catch bad commits, the way you structure a project so an agent can navigate it. Thoughtworks promoting this to a top-level theme in their most-read twice-yearly industry report is the signal that 'wire up your harness carefully' has moved from power-user advice to default practice — and the specific controls they endorse are concrete and copyable. Three practical things to notice. First, the feedforward controls they call out — GitHub Spec-Kit and OpenSpec — are both tools that force an agent to write a spec before writing code; worth looking at if you've been letting an agent run freely and getting surprised by what it ships. Second, the feedback control they call out — mutation testing — is a technique that generates small intentional bugs in your code and checks whether your test suite catches them. For Python, the `mutmut` and `cosmic-ray` libraries do this; running mutation tests against your own code is a sharper check than coverage percentage when you want to know whether your tests actually work. Third — new in the overnight reading — agent sandboxing moved from Trial to Adopt in this edition, which means Thoughtworks is now recommending by default that you run AI coding agents inside a restricted environment (a container, a VM, a scoped dev container, or at minimum a dedicated OS user) rather than on your main shell; for a Python project, the lightest-weight version of this is a `docker run --rm -v $PWD:/work` or a fresh devcontainer, and the strongest version is running the agent on a cloud machine you can throw away. Also worth noticing: the Radar explicitly cautions against defaulting to a frontier model for every task, which is a tooling-team consultancy of record saying that 'always use the biggest model' is the wrong default — this is the industry-adoption signal for the GitHub Copilot deprecation story in today's other item (configs pinning the biggest/newest model name are now the anti-pattern, not the best practice). More broadly: the fact that a consultancy advising Fortune 500s is now calling token economics 'infrastructure economics' is worth reading as a judgment that the dev-tools AI boom is a capital-intensive game, not a scrappy one, and that the sustainable individual practice is to build a careful, repeatable harness rather than chase whichever model is currently cheapest.
items.why_it_matters_brief: Thoughtworks' twice-yearly Radar promoted the control layer around AI coding agents from blip to theme, moved agent sandboxing from Trial to Adopt, and cautioned against defaulting to a frontier model for every task — 'wire up your harness carefully' is now the industry default, not power-user advice.

items.title: GitHub Copilot pulls Claude Opus 4.8, Claude Opus 5, and GPT-5.6 Terra on November 16 — eight days out, and the annual-plan carve-out is narrower than it looked
items.summary: GitHub's October 15, 2026 Copilot changelog entry announced that three models — Claude Opus 4.8, Claude Opus 5, and GPT-5.6 Terra — will be removed from every Copilot surface (Chat, inline editing, ask and agent modes, and code completion) on November 16, 2026, exactly eight days from the time of this enrichment pass. GitHub's recommended replacements: Claude Opus 5.5 in place of either Claude Opus 4.8 or Claude Opus 5, and GPT-6.1 Sol or GPT-6 Luna in place of GPT-5.6 Terra. Enterprise and Business admins get the replacements automatically enabled unless they've turned off the global default or disabled the model at the org level. There is one narrow exception to the cutoff: individual users on an annual Copilot plan can continue using Claude Opus 4.8 past November 16; no corresponding carve-out exists for Claude Opus 5 or GPT-5.6 Terra, and — new in the overnight reading — secondary coverage clarifies that monthly individual plans and all organization/enterprise plans lose Opus 4.8 on the same November 16 cutoff, so the annual-plan reprieve applies to a small subset of the user base rather than most users. GitHub emphasizes that anyone whose configuration files, scripts, or agent definitions reference the deprecated model names by their literal string — common in custom Skills files, agent YAML, or shell wrappers — needs to update those references before the cutoff, or those code paths will start failing when the models disappear from the picker and API. New overnight: GitHub has also clarified post-cutoff behavior in two ways: users who had manually selected one of the retiring models (overriding the Copilot default) will need to open the model picker and reselect a replacement on their own after November 16 — GitHub will not auto-pick for non-admin individual overrides; and admins should confirm the two replacement families (Opus 5.5 and the GPT-6 Sol/Luna pair) are enabled in their model policy settings now, because a disabled replacement at the org level will leave users with no working model after deprecation even though the deprecation is automated. The changelog is dated October 15, 2026, so this news has been live for about three and a half weeks, but the migration deadline is now imminent and no further grace period has been announced.
items.why_it_matters: This is the practical 'check your configs' reminder rather than a conceptual story, and the window is now a week and change. If any of your GitHub Copilot config files, custom agent definitions, Skills files, or shell wrappers reference 'claude-opus-5,' 'claude-opus-4-8,' or 'gpt-5.6-terra' by literal string, it will silently route to a fallback or break next Monday. For Gabe's HTML/CSS/Python work the direct relevance is narrower if you've been doing most of your AI coding inside the browser-based ChatGPT or Claude apps rather than through VS Code's Copilot integration — but if any project has a .github/copilot config, a custom agent YAML file, or a shell wrapper pinning one of those model names, next week is the migration window. Two practical post-overnight-reading additions: first, if you ever manually picked one of the retiring models in the Copilot model selector (overriding the default), GitHub won't silently switch you to a replacement — you'll need to open the picker and reselect on November 16 or later, so it's worth checking now whether any of your machines are in that state. Second, if you're using Copilot through any org or school account rather than an individual plan, confirm the admin has the Opus 5.5 and GPT-6 Sol/Luna families enabled in the model policy, because an org that forgets to flip those switches will leave everyone without a working Copilot model on cutoff day. The broader signal worth noticing is how fast the model-rotation cadence has become: Claude Opus 5 was Anthropic's top model about six weeks ago (September 22), and it's already being retired from GitHub Copilot to make room for Opus 5.5. The half-life of 'the newest frontier Claude or GPT model' in a major tooling platform is now measured in weeks, not months. This lines up with today's other item: Thoughtworks' Radar Vol 35 explicitly cautions against defaulting to a frontier model for every task, which is the bigger pattern this deprecation is a specific instance of — pinning version numbers of frontier models is an anti-pattern because those versions don't live long in production platforms. If you've been treating model-name references as semi-permanent, they aren't anymore; the practical workaround is to use GitHub's 'default model' setting and an alias indirection rather than pinning versions, and to prefer the family name (claude-opus-latest, gpt-6-latest) wherever the platform supports it. There's also an annual-plan carve-out specifically for Opus 4.8 that doesn't extend to Opus 5 or GPT-5.6 Terra and — overnight clarification — doesn't extend to monthly individual plans or org/enterprise plans either, so it's a narrow tail for a specific subset of annual subscribers rather than a universal reprieve.

items.title: NYT and three Tribune Publishing papers sue Brave Software over a 30-billion-page AI scraping index — Perplexity is the only named AI customer that has publicly commented, and 'overpaying its attorneys and underpaying its journalists' is the line
items.summary: On November 2, 2026, the New York Times Company and three Tribune Publishing papers — the Daily News, Chicago Tribune, and Orlando Sentinel — filed two parallel lawsuits in the Southern District of New York alleging that Brave Software built an index of more than 30 billion web pages, reportedly via an unidentified crawler, and resold access to that index to AI companies including Anthropic, Perplexity, Mistral, xAI, and Cohere. Case numbers: New York Times Co. v. Brave Software Inc., No. 1:26-cv-09549, and Daily News LP v. Brave Software Inc., No. 1:26-cv-09554. The complaints target three distinct Brave products — the Brave Search API, the Ask Brave AI answers feature, and the browser's Paywall-blocking functionality — and allege that Brave scraped paywalled journalism, that the publishers were unable to block Brave's crawler from indexing their sites, and that Brave's product helps readers get past paywalls. None of the AI companies named as customers in the filings is a defendant in the current suits. New overnight: of the five AI companies named as Brave customers, only Perplexity has publicly commented; a Perplexity spokesperson responded with 'The New York Times is overpaying its attorneys and underpaying its journalists.' Anthropic and xAI did not respond to requests for comment; Mistral and Cohere have not surfaced in secondary coverage either. Brave itself has also not publicly responded — the Times said it had written to Brave CEO Brendan Eich in August 2025 and April 2026 and received no response, so the silence pattern predates the suit. Brave's own AI marketing page previously described the Brave Index as holding 'over 30 billion webpages, with millions of new pages indexed each day' — the figure the complaints anchor the 30-billion claim to. Context: Brave sued News Corp in March 2025 seeking a declaration that its indexing constituted fair use, arguing it is 'fair use' to index website content 'which all search engine operators must do to exist'; News Corp filed a July 2026 countersuit over Wall Street Journal and New York Post content. The Brave suits add a new vector to the ongoing publisher-vs-AI legal fight — going after the data broker rather than the AI company that used the data.
items.why_it_matters: The interesting thing here is the theory of the case, not the headline. The NYT has had an active suit against OpenAI and Microsoft for roughly three years, and a parade of other publishers have filed similar cases against AI companies directly. Going after Brave instead is a bet that liability runs further up the data supply chain than most AI-company arguments have been willing to admit. If the publishers win, the practical effect is that AI companies lose a cheap path to building large general-purpose crawls — they'd either have to crawl themselves (with the blocking-and-robots.txt and bot-detection arms race that implies) or buy from a licensee rather than a broker. Two new wrinkles from overnight reading. First: Perplexity's response — 'The New York Times is overpaying its attorneys and underpaying its journalists' — is the only public reaction from any of the five AI companies named as Brave customers, and it's a combative framing (attack the plaintiff's legal strategy, don't engage with the substance of the alleged scraping chain) rather than a substantive defense. Anthropic and xAI have stayed quiet; that's worth noting because historically Anthropic has published usage-policy commentary when it's named in filings, and silence here might suggest it's evaluating whether to break with Perplexity's framing or quietly comply. Second: the complaints are broader than the AI-training story — they also target Brave's Paywall-blocking browser feature and the Ask Brave AI answers product, which means the lawsuit is as much about whether Brave's product can bypass paywalls at all as it is about whether the underlying index was lawfully built. That matters because a loss on the Paywall-blocking piece could set precedent for any browser extension or plugin that helps a reader get around a paywall — a category that overlaps with privacy and anti-tracking tools Gabe might use or build. For a hobbyist building personal projects with public data — a Python script that scrapes blog posts for a personal RAG pipeline, say — the direct relevance is small; your scale is too low to invite trouble. The broader signal: the training-data supply chain is now a contested legal surface, and 'we're just a search index' — which is roughly what Brave argued against News Corp in 2025 — is the same defense you'd use for a self-hosted scraper. Whether Brave wins on fair use or loses on a secondary-liability theory matters for whether the same pattern remains legal in 2027 and whether it gets more expensive for AI companies to source training data (which, in the long run, flows back to API prices).
items.why_it_matters_brief: Perplexity is the only named AI customer to comment on the NYT/Brave suit — 'overpaying its attorneys and underpaying its journalists' — while Anthropic, xAI, and Brave itself have stayed silent, and the complaints target the Paywall-blocking feature alongside the scraping index.

items.title: Baidu releases ERNIE 5.5 Flash Base weights — 280B MoE pretraining checkpoint, 33.5T training tokens, custom license with 'Powered by ERNIE' attribution requirement
items.summary: On November 5, 2026, Baidu's ERNIE team released the weights for ERNIE 5.5 Flash Base — a text-only mixture-of-experts pretraining checkpoint with roughly 280 billion total parameters activating about 14 billion per token, trained from scratch on 33.5 trillion tokens. The weights are available on Hugging Face (FP8 and BF16 variants at baidu/ERNIE-5.5-Flash-Base and baidu/ERNIE-5.5-Flash-Base-BF16) and on ModelScope. This is a base model intended for downstream fine-tuning, not a chat or instruct model; Baidu says a post-trained ERNIE 5.5 Flash will follow. The license is a custom agreement (ERNIE 5.5 Flash Base Model License Agreement v1.0), not a standard open-source license: commercial use below $50 million in annual revenue is allowed with a one-time notice and a 'Powered by ERNIE' attribution requirement; above that threshold, Baidu's separate written authorization is required. Baidu's own benchmark tables show ERNIE 5.5 Flash Base scoring 93.3% on MMLU against DeepSeek-V4-Flash-Base's 89.4%, though the comparisons are mixed — Hy3-preview-Base leads on FullStackBench and DeepSeek leads on InfiniteBench. Context window: 128K tokens during pretraining, with the model card citing up to 1 million tokens available for fine-tuning and inference. The Hugging Face widget reports 286B parameters (a different counting convention applied to the same files), and one source notes the HF repositories existed with minimal content since October 21 before receiving the full checkpoints on or around November 2.
items.why_it_matters:
This is a pretraining base checkpoint rather than a ready-to-use model, so the direct practical relevance depends on whether you're doing any fine-tuning work. If you're experimenting with training or fine-tuning smaller models, a well-trained base at this scale provides a starting point that someone else paid the compute for — which is the whole point of base checkpoint releases. The practical floor here is 'the base model for fine-tuning consumer-scale variants' rather than a model you'd load in its full 280B form on consumer hardware.

Two things worth noticing. First, the license is not standard open-source — it's Baidu's own agreement, and the 'Powered by ERNIE' attribution requirement is a commercial condition you'd need to track. For a personal project it's effectively permissive below $50M revenue, but it's not MIT or Apache 2.0, and that matters if you're ever putting a product on something built on top of this base. This is the same 'open weights but with conditions' pattern as Kimi K3.1 Pro last week (which requires the Kimi name on large products) and Mistral Large 4 (Mistral Ecosystem Open-Weight license, not plain MIT) — the broader trend is that labs are releasing weights with branding or use-restriction conditions rather than clean open-source terms, and you need to read the license file before assuming these are as free as Apache 2.0.

Second, Baidu releasing this at all is notable from an industry direction standpoint. For much of 2025 and early 2026, Baidu looked like it was moving toward closed API-only models as its competitive strategy. ERNIE 5.0 was API-only at launch; this is the first pretraining release in the ERNIE 5.x generation. That shift suggests Baidu is responding to the same open-weight competitive pressure that pushed Meta to open-source Muse Glimmer (August 2026) and Mistral to open-weight Large 4 (October 2026). The pattern across all three: labs with strong research pipelines are releasing pretraining checkpoints or near-inference weights not because they want to but because staying closed in a world where Kimi K3.1 Pro and Mistral Large 4 weights are freely downloadable makes you look like you're hiding something — or charging for access to something the ecosystem has decided should be free.
items.why_it_matters_brief: Baidu releases its first open-weight pretraining checkpoint of the ERNIE 5.x generation — a custom license (not Apache/MIT, requires 'Powered by ERNIE' attribution below $50M revenue), following the same 'open weights with marketing-string conditions' pattern as Kimi K3.1 Pro and Mistral Large 4.

revisions.change: created — Baidu ERNIE 5.5 Flash Base weights released Nov 5, 2026. 280B total / 14B active MoE pretraining checkpoint. 33.5T training tokens. FP8 and BF16 variants on Hugging Face (baidu/ERNIE-5.5-Flash-Base and baidu/ERNIE-5.5-Flash-Base-BF16) and ModelScope. Custom ERNIE 5.5 Flash Base Model License Agreement v1.0 — not standard open-source; commercial use below $50M with 'Powered by ERNIE' attribution; above requires Baidu's written authorization. Self-reported MMLU 93.3% vs DeepSeek-V4-Flash-Base 89.4%; mixed results across other benchmarks. Post-trained ERNIE 5.5 Flash chat model to follow. hero_image null (Baidu and HuggingFace domains unreachable from this agent's egress, consistent with prior runs).
